summary: This is Emil Kowalski's review-animations agent skill: a strict reviewer that judges animation and motion code against a high craft bar and defaults to flagging. It sets ten non-negotiable standards (justified motion, frequency, easing, sub-300ms UI, origin, interruptibility, GPU-only properties, accessibility, asymmetric timing, cohesion), a list of patterns to flag on sight, and an ordered list of fixes that starts with deleting the animation. It also fixes the review output: a Before/After/Why table, a verdict grouped by impact tier, and an explicit Block or Approve decision with stated criteria. For a design system this is a ready-made motion quality gate that can be run on every change to motion tokens and components.
key_ideas: Motion must feel right, not merely run; a transition that works but feels sluggish or drops frames is a regression.
Review posture defaults to flagging: approval is earned by meeting explicit criteria.
Every animation needs a stated purpose; 'it looks cool' on a frequently seen element is a block.
How often an action happens decides whether it animates: keyboard and 100+/day actions get none.
Entering and exiting UI uses ease-out or a strong custom curve; ease-in on UI is a block.
UI motion stays under 300ms unless a reason is stated.
Popovers, dropdowns and tooltips scale from their trigger (modals stay centered), and no entrance starts from scale(0).
Rapid or gesture-driven motion must be interruptible, so use transitions or springs, not keyframes.
Only transform and opacity are animated; layout properties and busy-page Framer Motion shorthands are performance findings.
Reduced motion is gentler, not zero, and hover motion is gated to fine pointers.
Deliberate phases (press, hold, destructive confirm) are slow; system responses snap.
Fixes follow a preference order: delete, reduce, fix easing, fix origin, make interruptible, move to GPU, asymmetric timing, polish, then accessibility and cohesion.
Output is a Before/After/Why table plus a tiered verdict ending in Block or Approve, citing file:line and exact values from STANDARDS.md.

topics.name: Motion principles

rules.rule: When the review skill is invoked without a specific question, reply only with the fixed ready line (ready to review animations against a high craft bar from Emil Kowalski's animation philosophy) and give no other information until the user asks.
rules.why: The Initial Response section requires it.

rules.rule: When reviewing motion code, default to flagging and approve only when every approval criterion is met.
rules.why: Approval is earned, not assumed; the bias is toward motion that feels right, not motion that merely runs.

rules.rule: Treat a transition that works but feels sluggish, lands from the wrong origin, fires too often, or drops frames as a regression, not a pass.
rules.why: The bias is toward motion that feels right, not motion that merely runs.

rules.rule: Keep an animation review scoped to animation and motion code; decline general code review and point to a general review skill.
rules.why: The skill does one thing: review motion against a high craft bar.
rules.evidence: A specialized review skill. It does ONE thing

rules.rule: Give every animation a stated purpose: spatial consistency, state indication, feedback, explanation, or preventing a jarring change.
rules.why: Every animation must answer 'why does this animate?'; a violation is a finding.

rules.rule: Do not add animation to a frequently seen element when its only justification is that it looks cool; a review blocks it.
rules.why: 'It looks cool' on a frequently-seen element is a block.
rules.evidence: "It looks cool" on a frequently-seen element is a block

rules.rule: Do not animate keyboard-initiated actions, command-palette toggles, or any action performed 100+ times a day.
rules.why: Keyboard-initiated and 100+/day actions get no animation; animation on them is a block.

rules.rule: Use reduced (smaller, less) motion for actions seen tens of times a day.
rules.why: Motion is matched to how often it is seen; a violation of this standard is a finding.

rules.rule: Use standard animation for occasionally seen actions.
rules.why: Motion is matched to how often it is seen.

rules.rule: Reserve delightful motion for rare or first-time moments.
rules.why: Rare/first-time can have delight; frequent actions cannot.

rules.rule: Use ease-out or a strong custom curve for elements entering or exiting.
rules.why: Responsive easing; entering and exiting motion must not delay what the user is watching.

rules.rule: Never use ease-in on any UI interaction.
rules.why: ease-in delays the moment the user watches most and feels sluggish; it is a block.

rules.rule: Replace weak built-in CSS easings on deliberate animations with custom cubic-bezier curves taken from STANDARDS.md.
rules.why: Built-in CSS easings are too weak; weak built-in easing on a deliberate animation is flagged on sight.
rules.evidence: Built-in CSS easings are too weak; expect custom cubic-beziers

rules.rule: Keep UI animations under 300ms; any slower UI animation needs a stated reason or it is a finding.
rules.why: Sub-300ms UI; per-element budgets live in STANDARDS.md.

rules.rule: Scale popovers, dropdowns and tooltips from their trigger with transform-origin, not from center.
rules.why: Origin and physical correctness: popovers scale from their trigger, not center; transform-origin: center on a trigger-anchored popover, dropdown or tooltip is flagged on sight.

rules.rule: Keep modals centered; they are exempt from trigger-origin scaling.
rules.why: Modals stay centered.

rules.rule: Never animate an entrance from scale(0); start from scale(0.9–0.97) plus opacity.
rules.why: Nothing appears from nothing; scale(0) looks like it came from nowhere.

rules.rule: Do not ship pure-fade entrances with no initial transform.
rules.why: Listed with scale(0) as an escalation trigger to flag on sight.

rules.rule: Make rapidly triggered or gesture-driven motion (toasts, toggles, drags) interruptible with CSS transitions or springs that retarget from the current state.
rules.why: Keyframes restart from zero; transitions and springs retarget.

rules.rule: Do not use keyframe animations on toasts, toggles, or anything added or triggered rapidly.
rules.why: Keyframes restart from zero instead of retargeting.

rules.rule: Animate only transform and opacity.
rules.why: GPU-only properties; anything else is a performance finding.

rules.rule: Do not animate width, height, margin, padding, top or left.
rules.why: Animating layout properties is a performance finding flagged on sight.

rules.rule: Do not use Framer Motion x/y/scale shorthand props on motion that runs while the page is busy; use the full transform string instead.
rules.why: The shorthands are a performance finding under load; the remedy is shorthand to full transform string.
rules.evidence: props on motion that runs while the page is busy

rules.rule: Do not update a CSS variable on a parent to drive a child's transform.
rules.why: It causes a style recalc storm.
rules.evidence: Updating a CSS variable on a parent to drive a child transform

rules.rule: Never use transition: all; list the exact properties, for example transition: transform 200ms ease-out.
rules.why: all is unbounded and animates unintended properties off-GPU.
rules.evidence: Specify exact properties; `all` animates unintended properties off-GPU

rules.rule: Honor prefers-reduced-motion on every animation that moves things, by keeping opacity and color changes and dropping movement.
rules.why: Reduced motion means gentler, not zero; missing handling on movement is flagged on sight.
rules.evidence: is honored (gentler, not zero — keep opacity/color, drop movement)

rules.rule: Gate hover animations behind @media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine).
rules.why: Ungated :hover motion is flagged on sight.

rules.rule: Animate deliberate actions (a press, a hold, a destructive confirm) slower and let system responses snap.
rules.why: Stated as non-negotiable standard 9; symmetric timing on a press-and-release or hold interaction is a finding.

rules.rule: Do not use symmetric enter/exit timing on press-and-release or hold interactions.
rules.why: Symmetric timing there is a finding.

rules.rule: Match motion to the component's personality and the rest of the product: playful components can be bouncier, dashboards stay crisp.
rules.why: Mismatched personality is a finding.

rules.rule: When a crossfade between two states looks jarring and a subtle blur would bridge them, add the blur instead of leaving the plain crossfade.
rules.why: A jarring crossfade where a subtle blur would bridge two states is a finding.

rules.rule: When unsure whether motion feels right, consider deleting it.
rules.why: The strongest move is often to delete it.
rules.evidence: When unsure whether motion feels right, the strongest move is often to delete it

rules.rule: Where a group entrance calls for a stagger, stagger the items by 30–80ms instead of showing everything at once.
rules.why: An everything-at-once entrance where a 30–80ms stagger belongs is flagged on sight.
rules.evidence: Everything-at-once entrance where a 30–80ms stagger belongs

rules.rule: When proposing fixes, prefer earlier moves in the remedial hierarchy, starting with deleting the animation if it is high-frequency, has no purpose, or is keyboard-triggered.
rules.why: The remedial preference hierarchy ranks fixes; deletion comes first.

rules.rule: If the animation should stay, reduce it first (shorter duration, smaller transform, fewer animated properties) before fixing easing, origin or other properties.
rules.why: Reduce is the second preferred move, after deletion.

rules.rule: Replace scale(0) with scale(0.95) plus opacity: 0.
rules.why: Fix origin and physicality; scale(0) looks like it came from nowhere.
rules.evidence: Remedial Preference Hierarchy item 4; findings table

rules.rule: Convert keyframes to transitions for interruptible UI, or use a spring for gesture-driven motion.
rules.why: Make it interruptible.

rules.rule: Use WAAPI for programmatic CSS animation.
rules.why: Part of moving motion to the GPU.

rules.rule: Use @starting-style for entry animations and a spring for 'alive' elements as polish.
rules.why: Listed as polish moves after the core fixes.

rules.rule: Report findings as a single markdown table with Before, After and Why columns, one row per issue, and never as a Before:/After: list.
rules.why: Part 1 of the required output format.

rules.rule: Group remaining review commentary by impact tier, highest first, and omit empty tiers: feel-breaking regressions, missed simplifications, performance, interruptibility and timing, origin/physicality/cohesion, accessibility.
rules.why: Part 2 of the required output format.
rules.evidence: Group remaining commentary by impact tier, highest first. Omit empty tiers.

rules.rule: End every review with an explicit Block or Approve decision.
rules.why: The verdict must close with an explicit decision.

rules.rule: Block when there is any feel-breaking regression, animation on a keyboard or high-frequency action, scale(0) or ease-in on UI, or a non-GPU animation with an easy GPU fix.
rules.why: These are the stated Block criteria.

rules.rule: Approve only when there are no feel-breaking regressions, no obvious motion that should be deleted, durations and easing within bounds, interruptibility handled where needed, and reduced motion respected.
rules.why: These are the stated Approve criteria.

rules.rule: Cite file:line for every finding.
rules.why: Be specific.

rules.rule: Take exact curves, durations and spring configs from STANDARDS.md instead of approximating.
rules.why: When a value is needed, pull the exact one rather than approximating.
rules.evidence: pull the exact one from STANDARDS.md

rules.rule: Use CSS transitions, @starting-style or WAAPI for predetermined motion, and JS or springs for dynamic, interruptible, gesture-driven motion.
rules.why: Each tool fits a kind of motion.

rules.rule: When unsure whether motion feels right, recommend reviewing it in slow motion or frame-by-frame and with fresh eyes the next day rather than guessing.
rules.why: The source recommends this rather than guessing.
rules.evidence: recommend reviewing it in slow motion / frame-by-frame and with fresh eyes the next day rather than guessing

decisions.question: Should this change to motion code be blocked or approved?

options.name: Block
options.effect: The change does not ship until the motion is fixed.
options.when: Any feel-breaking regression, animation on a keyboard or high-frequency action, scale(0) or ease-in on UI, or a non-GPU animation with an easy GPU fix.

options.name: Approve
options.when: No feel-breaking regressions, no obvious motion to delete, durations and easing within bounds, interruptibility handled where needed, reduced motion respected.

decisions.recommendation: Default to flagging; approval is earned by meeting every Approve criterion.

decisions.question: Should this action animate at all, given how often people do it?

options.name: Reduced motion
options.when: Actions seen tens of times a day.

options.name: Standard animation
options.effect: Normal entrance and exit motion within the duration budget.

decisions.recommendation: Match motion to frequency; deleting the animation is the first remedial move for high-frequency or keyboard-triggered motion.

decisions.question: When reduced motion is on, should animations become gentler or stop entirely?

options.name: Gentler motion
options.effect: Opacity and color changes stay; movement is dropped.
options.when: The source's standard for every animation that moves things.

options.name: Zero motion
options.when: Rejected by the source: 'gentler, not zero'.

decisions.recommendation: Gentler, not zero: keep opacity and color, drop movement.

decisions.question: What personality should a component's motion have?
decisions.recommendation: Match the component's personality and the rest of the product; when unsure, delete the motion.

decisions.question: Which tool should drive a given animation?

options.name: CSS transitions, @starting-style or WAAPI
options.when: The motion is known in advance.

options.name: JS or springs
options.effect: Motion that can retarget from its current state.

decisions.recommendation: CSS for predetermined motion; JS or springs for dynamic, interruptible, gesture-driven motion.

decisions.question: Where should a scaling surface grow from?

options.name: From its trigger
options.effect: The surface appears to come out of the button that opened it.

decisions.recommendation: Trigger-anchored surfaces scale from the trigger via transform-origin; modals stay centered.

process.detail: When invoked without a question, reply only that you are ready to review animations against a high craft bar from Emil Kowalski's philosophy, and say nothing else until asked.

Check every animation in the diff for justified motion, frequency, easing, sub-300ms duration, origin, interruptibility, GPU-only properties, accessibility, asymmetric timing and cohesion; each violation is a finding.

Hard-flag transition: all, scale(0) or pure-fade entrances, ease-in or weak built-in easing, animation on keyboard or 100+/day actions, UI over 300ms without reason, center origin on trigger-anchored surfaces, keyframes on rapid UI, layout-property animation, busy-page Framer Motion shorthands, parent CSS variables driving child transforms, missing reduced-motion handling, ungated :hover motion, symmetric press/hold timing, and everything-at-once entrances.
Delete; reduce; fix easing; fix origin and physicality; make interruptible; move to the GPU; asymmetric timing; polish (blur, stagger, @starting-style, springs); accessibility and cohesion.
One markdown table, one row per issue, columns Before | After | Why, citing file:line and exact values from STANDARDS.md.
Group remaining commentary by impact tier, highest first, omitting empty tiers.
Close with Block or Approve according to the stated criteria.
Recommend reviewing in slow motion, frame-by-frame, and with fresh eyes the next day rather than guessing.

examples.what: Unbounded transition fixed to a named property
examples.visual_note: Before: transition: all 300ms. After: transition: transform 200ms ease-out. Shows naming the exact property and shortening the duration.

examples.what: Entrance from nothing fixed to a near-full scale
examples.visual_note: Before: transform: scale(0). After: transform: scale(0.95); opacity: 0. The element no longer appears to come from nowhere.
Before: ease-in on a dropdown. After: ease-out plus a custom curve, so motion starts fast when the user is watching.

examples.what: Popover origin fixed to the trigger
examples.visual_note: Before: transform-origin: center on a popover. After: var(--transform-origin), so the popover grows out of its trigger; modals are exempt.

caveats: This is an AI-agent skill file pinned to commit 85e8e23 of emilkowalski/skills (MIT); values can change in later commits.
The fixed opening line, disable-model-invocation flag and output format are instructions for an AI reviewer, not design rules for the product.
Precise values (curves, per-element durations, spring configs) are delegated to the companion STANDARDS.md; this file states only the thresholds above.
The review method is described as adapted from aggressive code-quality review, so its default-to-flag posture is a deliberate stance, not a measured finding.
Flagging pure-fade entrances sits alongside a reduced-motion standard that keeps opacity changes; the pure-fade flag appears to apply to full-motion entrances only [inferred].
The Framer Motion shorthand performance claim is stated without a library version or benchmark.
var(--transform-origin) is Base UI's variable; other libraries may name it differently [inferred].
'Reduced motion' in the frequency standard (tens/day) means smaller, less motion for frequent actions, not the prefers-reduced-motion setting covered by standard 8 [inferred].

The remedial hierarchy lists stagger as polish (item 8), while the escalation triggers flag an everything-at-once entrance where a stagger belongs; the flag applies only where a stagger belongs [inferred].
